title: Checkpoint: Ancestors, Kami and the Land
objective: After this level you can connect ancestors, kami and sacred land into a picture of traditions that live through ritual and place more than creed.
summary: Ancestor altars, shrines of kami, sacred mountains and returning ancestors: Chapter 7's traditions live through ritual and place more than creed.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: an altar, a gate, a mountain and a mask.
cards.body: From China to Japan, from Arizona to Australia to Nigeria, these traditions look very different. Lay them side by side and one pattern shows.

cards.headline: Ritual and place more than creed
cards.body: Notice what these traditions stress. The Association of Shinto Shrines says Shinto has no founder, no dogma and no doctrine. Tjukurpa is memorised and passed on to the right people. Ifa's knowledge passes among its priests, who are consulted for important decisions. In each, a tradition lives in rites and places, and in the people who carry it on. Places stay alive in belief too: in Pew's 2023 survey, about half of adults or more in Taiwan, Japan and Vietnam said mountains, rivers or trees have their own spirits.

questions.prompt: In Pew's 2023 survey, what did about half of adults or more in Taiwan, Japan and Vietnam say?

options.label: That they had never once visited a shrine or temple of any kind
That mountains, rivers or trees have their own spirits
That they belong to one official religion
options.rationale: Many say they have no religion.

options.label: That ancestors should not be honored

questions.explanation: Beliefs about sacred places run deep: many see spirits in mountains, rivers and trees.

questions.prompt: What do Chinese Qingming and Yoruba Egungun festivals have in common?

options.label: Both honor the ancestors
Both are held on the spring equinox
Both rebuild a shrine every 20 years
Both are led by the babalawo

questions.explanation: At Qingming families visit their ancestors' tombs; at Egungun the ancestors return in masquerade.

questions.prompt: Why do many Japanese take part in both Shinto and Buddhist rites?

options.label: A national law has long required every family to take part in both religions
They were combined for centuries, and each marks different moments of life
Shinto has no rites of its own
options.rationale: It has purification, festivals and childhood rites.

options.label: Buddhism forbids funerals

questions.explanation: Kami and buddhas were joined until 1868; shrines mark early life, while most funerals are Buddhist.

questions.prompt: Which Chapter 7 tradition is memorised and passed on to the right people, not written down?

options.label: The Qingming festival
options.rationale: Qingming is a festival, not a body of law.

options.label: The Association of Shinto Shrines' doctrine
options.rationale: The Association says Shinto has no doctrine.

options.label: Pure Land devotion
options.rationale: That's a school of Buddhism in China.

options.label: Anangu Tjukurpa

questions.explanation: Anangu describe Tjukurpa as memorised and passed on to the right people, like an inheritance.

questions.prompt: Level 8 said each Indigenous tradition belongs to its own people and land. Which Chapter 7 example shows that best?

options.label: The three teachings of China sharing one sky, like sun, moon and planets
The four sacred mountains that surround the Diné homeland
The mikoshi carried through a neighborhood
The name tablets on a Chinese altar

questions.explanation: Dinétah's four mountains belong to one people's stories and one people's land.
